title: ASP.NET Core
sub: No context, HttpContext lives until the request ends, work after the response goes to a BackgroundService
cards/0/title: What you already know: there is no context
cards/0/body:
From unit 4: in ASP.NET Core SynchronizationContext.Current == null. Any free pool thread runs the continuation after await, so the classic .Result deadlock doesn't happen. For the same reason ConfigureAwait(false) changes nothing in application code: there's nothing to capture and nowhere to return to. Libraries use it for callers that come from WPF or Unity.

But .Result hurts in Core too. While the database replies, the pool thread taken for the request just stands there doing nothing. Under load this produces an almost-deadlock, the pool starvation from u4.l5: every thread is stuck on .Result, and the continuations that would free them wait in the same pool queue behind new requests. Responses take seconds while the CPU sits idle.
cards/0/deep:
Why old ASP.NET hung. Old ASP.NET (.NET Framework) hung differently from WPF. It has no UI thread, but it does have a context: AspNetSynchronizationContext. It isn't a single thread but a rule: only one thread at a time runs inside a request's context. Step by step:

  • 1. The pool thread that took the request calls GetUserAsync; the await inside captures the request context.
  • 2. That thread blocks on .Result and keeps occupying the request context the whole time.
  • 3. The database replies. The continuation has to enter the request context, but a thread is already in there: the one blocked on .Result.
  • 4. Each waits for the other: a deadlock, even though a server has no "main" thread at all. This request and its thread hang; other requests are still served.

That's why libraries for old ASP.NET used ConfigureAwait(false): a continuation without a context doesn't need to enter the request, so the cycle never closes.
cards/1/task: An ASP.NET Core request handler calls .Result. The top lane is the thread running the handler: on a server it's also a pool thread taken for the request. Run it to the end: will it hang?
cards/2/task: Rewrite the handler with await and run it to the end. Watch what the request thread does while the reply is on its way.
cards/3/q: ASP.NET Core on .NET 8, 8 cores. Every request does _repo.GetAsync(id).Result, and the database replies in 20 ms. 300 requests arrive at once: the CPU is at 5%, yet responses take 10-20 seconds. Why so long, if a deadlock is impossible in ASP.NET Core?
cards/3/options/0: Threads are stuck on .Result, and the continuations that would free them wait in the pool queue behind new requests; the pool adds new threads with pauses
cards/3/options/1: Without a SynchronizationContext a continuation runs only after the request has sent its response
cards/3/options/2: Application code has no ConfigureAwait(false), so continuations wait for the request context
cards/3/explain: This is the almost-deadlock from u4.l5: the cycle breaks once the pool grows enough, but until then requests stand still. ConfigureAwait(false) is irrelevant: Core has no context. The cure is await all the way.
cards/4/body:
After await, a controller method may be resumed by a different pool thread. That's fine for HttpContext: it's an ordinary object the controller references (the HttpContext property), not something tied to a thread. Until the request ends, HttpContext is available after any await, including after ConfigureAwait(false).

Old ASP.NET was different: the static HttpContext.Current was restored by AspNetSynchronizationContext, so after ConfigureAwait(false) it became null. Core has no HttpContext.Current.
cards/5/q: An ASP.NET Core controller. What happens on the HttpContext line?
cards/5/options/0: It works: the request is still running, HttpContext is an ordinary object, and it doesn't matter which pool thread resumed the method
cards/5/options/2: InvalidOperationException: HttpContext may only be touched from the thread that accepted the request
cards/5/explain: Thread affinity belonged to HttpContext.Current in old ASP.NET. In Core HttpContext is a controller property, and it's alive until the request ends.
cards/6/body:
The thread doesn't matter, but two rules remain:

  • 1. HttpContext isn't thread-safe. Sequential awaits are fine. Two parallel branches (WhenAll) that both read the request body or write headers are a race.
  • 2. HttpContext lives only until the request ends. After the response the server resets it and may hand the same object to the next request. A background task holding a reference reads someone else's data or empty fields, or gets ObjectDisposedException.

If a service needs HttpContext, it uses IHttpContextAccessor. It keeps a reference to a shared holder with the context in an AsyncLocal, so the value travels through await together with ExecutionContext (u3.l4). When the request ends, the server clears the holder itself, and accessor.HttpContext returns null, even in a task that inherited the ExecutionContext.
cards/7/q: AuditService (through IHttpContextAccessor) started a Task.Run from a request. The task reads accessor.HttpContext a minute later, long after the response went out. What does it get?
cards/7/options/0: null: when the request ended, the server cleared the holder that every copy of the ExecutionContext shares
cards/7/options/1: Its own request's HttpContext: the AsyncLocal was copied into the task along with the ExecutionContext
cards/7/options/2: The HttpContext of whatever request the server is handling right now
cards/7/explain: The AsyncLocal did travel into the task, but what it holds isn't the HttpContext itself, it's a reference to a holder. When the request ends, the server clears the holder, and everyone referencing it sees null. Copy the data you need while the request is running.
cards/7/wrong/1: The reference made it, but to a holder the server cleared when the request ended.
cards/7/wrong/2: An AsyncLocal travels with the call chain, it doesn't live in a thread: another request's context won't show up in it.
cards/8/body:
The user closed the tab, and the server keeps running a heavy database query for a response nobody will receive. That's what the request's HttpContext.RequestAborted token is for: the server cancels it when the client drops the connection.

You don't need to type HttpContext.RequestAborted yourself. If a controller action or a minimal API handler has a CancellationToken parameter, ASP.NET Core passes exactly this token into it. From there it's u2.l5: pass it to every async call.

What happens on disconnect:

  • 1. The server cancels the token.
  • 2. The database driver or HttpClient that received the token aborts the operation and throws OperationCanceledException.
  • 3. The exception propagates up, no response is written: the client is gone. There's no need to treat it as an error.

Be careful with writes: if an operation must finish even without the client (the money is already charged, the order must be saved), don't give it RequestAborted.
cards/9/q: Abort the search if the client leaves
cards/9/explain: ASP.NET Core binds a CancellationToken parameter to HttpContext.RequestAborted. CancellationToken.None is never cancelled.
cards/10/title: Work after the response: your own scope and a queue
cards/10/body:
DI in ASP.NET Core creates scoped services once per request and disposes them when the request ends. The typical scoped service is EF Core's DbContext: it holds a database connection and isn't thread-safe.

What happens with _ = Task.Run(() => _db.SaveChangesAsync()) in a controller:

  • 1. Task.Run queues the lambda to the pool, and the controller returns Ok right away.
  • 2. The request ends, and DI disposes this request's DbContext.
  • 3. The lambda touches the disposed DbContext: ObjectDisposedException ("Cannot access a disposed context instance"). And if it started before the request finished its own database work, two operations run on one DbContext at once: a race.
  • 4. The exception sits in a task nobody awaits (u2.l3) and is lost.

The right way is to split the work. The request copies the data it needs into a queue and responds. A separate long-lived worker drains the queue and creates its own scope, with its own DbContext, for each item. The queue is a Channel from unit 5, the worker is a BackgroundService (next card).
cards/11/explain: The scoped DbContext is disposed when the request ends, but the background task will still use it, or use it at the same time as the request. And nobody will see the error.
cards/12/title: BackgroundService and IHostedService from the inside
cards/12/body:
IHostedService is a two-method interface: the host calls StartAsync when the app starts and StopAsync when it stops. BackgroundService is a ready-made implementation for a long-running loop: you only write ExecuteAsync(stoppingToken).

  • 1. On startup, StartAsync calls ExecuteAsync, stores its task and doesn't wait for it: the app keeps starting.
  • 2. The loop in ExecuteAsync lives as long as the app runs.
  • 3. On shutdown, StopAsync cancels stoppingToken and waits for the ExecuteAsync task, but no longer than the host's shutdown timeout (HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout, 30 s by default).

A hosted service lives as a singleton, so it can't take a scoped service through its constructor: in Development DI reports an error right away, and without that check the DbContext would live forever and be shared across threads. You create the scope yourself with IServiceScopeFactory.CreateAsyncScope(), and await using (u5.l4) disposes it together with the DbContext.

Since .NET 6, an exception escaping ExecuteAsync stops the whole app by default (HostOptions.BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior = StopHost). So you catch a single item's error inside the loop and let OperationCanceledException through on shutdown.
cards/12/deep:
Up to and including .NET 9, the synchronous part of ExecuteAsync (everything before the first await that actually waits) ran right inside StartAsync, during host startup (recall u2.l1: until its first pause an async method is an ordinary method). Long synchronous code there delayed the start of the other services. In .NET 10 the whole of ExecuteAsync runs in the background.

The exception behavior is configurable: with the Ignore value, the host just logs the error instead of stopping. But then the failed loop silently stops working while the app looks alive.
cards/13/q: The try/catch around SendAsync was removed from EmailWorker. One day the SMTP server returned an error and SendAsync threw. What happens on .NET 8?
cards/13/options/0: The exception completes the ExecuteAsync task, and the host stops the whole app
cards/13/options/1: The exception is swallowed, and the loop moves on to the next email
cards/13/options/2: The host restarts ExecuteAsync from the beginning
cards/13/explain: Since .NET 6 a failed BackgroundService stops the host by default. Catch a single email's error inside the loop.
